ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The Altotiberina Fault is a low-angle normal fault depicted by surface geology, boreholes and seismic profiles that extends along the inner Umbria region for a length of about 70 km, showing a mean N150Â°E direction and dipping ENE to a depth of 12-14 km beneath the Umbria-Marche fold-and-thrust belt (Barchi et al., 1999; Boncio et al., 1998 and 2000). Comparison between geological and seismological data confirms the Altotiberina Fault geometry and activity, suggesting its role as an active extensional structure that represents the basal detachment of the west dipping seismogenic normal faults of the Umbria-Marche region. Despite the large amount of evidences along its northern part, the Altotiberina Fault has weaker constraints along the Umbria Valley but it is strongly supposed to bound the western side of the basin and to present west dipping normal faults as antithetic ones (Boncio et al., 2000a and 2000b; Collettini et al, 2000; Mirabella et al., 2002). There are no sufficient data to state if the Altotiberina Fault is also able to produce moderate magnitude earthquake or if it creeps accompanied by microseismicity. Boncio et al. (2000b) propose that its shallowest hanging wall block is active, generating frequent clustering of microseismicity, seismic swarms and small magnitude earthquakes (even on the base of historical earthquake locations).
We suspect that some of the geomorphic and geologic evidence of lateral discontinuities (Gregori, 1988; Bonini, 1998) could play the role of geometric barriers in the propagation of earthquake rupture.
This source is associated with the Bastia 12 Febbraio 1854, I max=VII-VIII, historical earthquake (CPTI, Working Group, 1999).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Could the Altotiberina low angle normal fault have a direct seismogenic role or does it mainly creep by means of stable frictional sliding?
2) Is the Altotiberina Fault capable of producing large or even moderate magnitude earthquakes?
3) Could the Altotiberina Fault be seismogenic along discrete segments, both confined by lateral discontinuities and in coincidence of steeper fault plane dips?
4) In correspondence of the historical earthquakes is the seismogenic layer (Altotiberina hanging wall) thick enough to nucleate moderate earthquakes?
5) Could historical earthquakes located close to the Altotiberina Fault trace be nucleated by the activity of antithetic segments?
sections.SUMMARIES:
GE.MI.NA. (1963)
This paper, based on drillings and geophysical data, studied the fluvio-lacustrine infill sequence of the Umbria basin: the basal Upper Pliocene gravelly-sandy complex, 300-600 m thick, presents lignite beds outcropping at Morgnano, Torgiano and Deruta towns; the clayey pre-Mindel Pleistocene complex, 400 m thick, presenting lignite beds, outcrops at Bastardo and Montefalco town; the sandy-clayey Gunz-Mindel complex, 300 m thick presents lignite beds outcropping at Bastardo and Bevagna; the upper gravelly-sandy complex lies on top of the infill sequence. Lignite beds outcrop exclusively along the western flank of the Umbria Valley. A reconstruction of the geometry of the bedrock/infill contact is also provided. The pre-lacustrine basement deepens toward the north-western part of the Umbria Valley. Its north-eastern flank is the steepest, probably due to a main, south-west dipping, normal fault plane. As evidence of significant antithetic, north-east dipping, normal fault activity, are highlighted: the Morgnano lignite, even if older, is topographically higher than the Bastardo lignite and its beds dip toward east due to a supposed fault or to a depocentre migration; near the Bastardo town, the dip of the lignite beds increases down-section and NW-SE trending faults affecting the lacustrine sequence were recognized.
Gregori (1988)
The Authors focus on the geomorphology of the Bastardo area (western side of the Umbria Valley) and recognize the presence of well preserved paleosurfaces, SW dipping, without ancient erosional features. They show how some piracies by NW flowing streams seems to be aligned with fault directions. A tilting toward SW of the sandy-gravelly complex is evidenced. They describe the Bastardo basin syncline-shaped surface and its independence with respect to the Umbria Valley.
They map many geomorphologic features, linked to NW-SE recently active faults, and indicate the presence of presumable tectonic breccias along the south-western edge of the basin. The Authors provide a tentative reconstruction of the evolution history of the Umbria basin: main W dipping faults, bounding the eastern flank of the Umbria Valley operated since Pliocene; during the Plio-Pleistocene, NW-SE trending, antithetic and synthetic faults affecting the Bastardo area, created a satellite basin characterised by general tilting toward SW of the continental deposits and consequent ponding; during the Lower Pleistocene, the lacustrine environment gradually disappeared due to the eastward migration of the catchments of the western hydrographic basin.
Cencetti (1990)
A geomorphologic and neo-tectonic map of the northern termination of the Mt. Martani chain is provided. Noting that the watershed is shifted toward east with respect to the structural axis of the Mt. Martani fold, a lithologic control on the morphogenic processes is evidenced. Some geomorphic features suggests the presence of NW-SE, synthetic and antithetic, normal faults.
The eastern side of the Tiber Valley exhibits evidences of recent tectonic activity: 40Â° SW-dipping beds of the sandy-gravelly; normal fault system lowering progressively toward SSW the Pleistocene deposits.
Barchi et al. (1991)
Meso-structural analyses were applied on continental deposits of the Umbria Valley. Many N140Â° trending mesoscopic faults, displacing Plio-Pleistocene deposits, together with joint systems, have been observed. A relevant tilting of the fluvial-lacustrine upper-conglomerates toward SSW has been evidenced near the western side of the Umbria Valley. The Authors, interpreting some commercial seismic lines, highlights: a planar trajectory, up to the depth of 8 km, of the SW-dipping master normal fault that bounds the eastern side of the Umbria Valley; a distinct WNW-ESE Bastardo basin, that present an eastern threshold separating it from the Umbria Valley; the presence of east dipping normal faults that bound the western side of the Bastardo basin; similar 500 m thickness of both basins, without evident asymmetry of the filling deposits.
Noting the relevance of the erosional processes with respect to sedimentary processes, the greatest part of the main normal faults offset is supposed to be related to uplift of the foot-wall blocks. A N50Â° Plio-Pleistocene extension direction, able to reactivate N10Â° trending pre-existing Miocene-Pliocene as left-lateral structures, is hypothesised.
Bonini (1997)
The Author analyses tectonic meso-structures, coupled with analyses of gravel slickenside rakes, to determine the direction of main stress, that affected the continental deposits of the Umbria basin. On the basis of such structural data, the Tiber basin and the Umbria basin are interpreted as originally developed on synclines, subsequently affected by an alternating stress regime: a Lower Pleistocene extensional phase; a compressional phase between the Lower Pleistocene and the Middle Pleistocene; a Middle-Upper Pleistocene phase, characterised by a NW-SE maximum compression, accompanied with a NE-SW maximum extension, that reactivated well-oriented NNW-SSE and NNE-SSW faults, which display normal and left-lateral kinematics, respectively. The importance of a NW-SE, SW dipping master fault, bounding the east side of the Umbria Valley is evidenced, together with the presence of NNE-SSW oriented structures transversal to the basin axis.
The Plio-Pleistocene Umbria basin deposits are tilted toward east due to the action of the master fault. The Author observed antithetic NW-SE striking normal faults, east dipping, bounding the western flank of the basin and affecting the Pleistocene lignite.
Barchi et al. (1998)
The history of the CROP 03 project along with the geophysical results achieved is presented in this paper. Data from NVR seismic, refraction seismic, passive seismic, gravimeter, magnetic and heat flow are described, discussed and presented by means of an interpreted profile crossing NE-SW the entire Central Italy, from Punta Ala to Gabicce village. On this basis, a geodynamic scenario envisages an Apennines domain in which compressive tectonics has acted since the Middle Miocene, whereas is now collapsing. The main deep features of the Tiber Valley area are: a westward dip of a thick Adriatic crust (about 35 km) in-between the Marchean foothills and the Tiber Valley; an antiformal stack of crustal slivers in-between the Valdichiana-Valtiberina; an east-dipping Valtiberina normal fault, which develops along the outer limb of the antiformal crustal stack, traceable at depth till about 13 km beneath the Umbro-Marchean Apennines. The tectonic system consist of a master fault, responsible for the formation of the Tiber Valley half graben, and of a family of antithetic faults resulting in a domino-like structure and connected to the grabens of Gubbio and Gualdo Tadino. The geodynamic meaning of this fault system, in spite of its clear geometry and present kinematics, is open to some question: the position of the master fault, localised in the forelimb of the crustal antiformal stack, would suggest a collapse phenomenon of the orogenic building as the tectonic setting of western domain displays; the low-angle east-dipping normal fault might have reactivated a former back-trust to stretch the crust, when, after the Oligocene, the subduction flipped and the convergence rate became consequently lower than the subduction roll-back.
Boncio et al. (1998)
These workers describe the geometry of the NNW-SSE trending, east-dipping, Altotiberina fault and of some antithetic splays. The work is based on field evidence and on interpretation of two commercial seismic lines, from the Tiber Valley to the Umbria-Marche Apennines, south of the CROP 03 line. The Altotiberina fault exhibits a staircase trajectory, starting as a steep, shallow fault below the Tiber Valley to the W and the becoming an almost flat surface to the E.
Its dip angle is low-medium (30Â°-40Â°) below the carbonate formations, at its eastern edge. Detailed microseismic data supplied by the 1991-1994 recordings of the local Umbria seismic network, by a temporary network set up soon after the 29 April 1984 M 5.2 Gubbio earthquake and during May-June 1987, are also used for understanding the relationships between the Altotiberina fault and regional seismicity. The distribution of seismic activity appears to be controlled by the Altotiberina fault, which separates an active hanging wall block, slipping towards the NE, from an almost aseismic foot wall block. Frequent microearthquakes and moderate size earthquakes are related to the activity of antithetic fault splays, such as the Gubbio fault. The interpretation of two seismic profiles shows an active wedge-shaped rock volume, whose base deepens eastward. The seismicity of the Tiber Valley, of the Gubbio area and of the Umbria Valley is concentrated around 6 km depth and tends to deepen towards the ENE, up to about 12 km beneath the Apennine chain. The authors point out that seismicity tends to concentrate exactly where the main antithetic faults (Gubbio and Colfiorito) intersect the Altotiberina fault, at about 6 km depth. In summary, this seismotectonic study identifies a highly seismic crustal block located east of the westernmost main antithetic faults. This crustal block is characterised by small to moderate earthquakes and by frequent microseismicity mainly clustered in the foot wall of the main antithetic faults, especially near their branch point. A second crustal block, west of the main antithetic faults, has a relatively aseismic behaviour. Such antithetic faults play a role of release-fault between both blocks and the shallow microseismicity located in their hanging wall is interpreted as the result of adjustment processes due to the collapse.
Bonini (1998)
A geologic-structural study of the plio-pleistocene continental Tiber basin has been carried out allowing to establish the role of strike-slip, compressional and extensional deformations affecting the deposits during the basin evolution. On the basis of field mapping and structural analysis, the development during Lower-Middle Pliocene of the three branches of the Tiber lake (Upper Tiber basin, Middle Tiber basin and Umbria basin) has been referred to a compressive regime.
During Lower Pleistocene the Tiber Basin was controlled by NW-SE trending normal faults cross-cutting obliquely the NNW trending older branches. The area was further affected by a NE-oriented shortening phase between Lower and Middle Pleistocene. The Pleistocene evolution of this sector has been also investigated by means of analogue modelling experiments, whose results support the hypothesised tectonic progression. A succession of NE to ENE-trending direction of compression or extension led to the reactivation of suitably-oriented pre-existing tectonic structures. The Umbria Valley continental basin is developed on a syncline structure, whose depression is bounded by normal faults and filled by Middle Pleistocene-Holocene alluvial deposits. This depression is delimited southward by a NNE-trending fault. This fault is interpreted as dextral lateral ramp formed during the Upper Miocene-Pliocene thrusting phase, afterward reactivated as sinistral, during the Middle Pleistocene extensional phase.
Sani et al. (1998)
Geologic-structural studies were performed in the internal basin of the Northern Apennines. This analysis led to recognise some main compressive event, affecting the continental sedimentary sequences and producing sedimentary unconformities. A transect crossing the Tiber basin was investigated, too. The Martani Mts. Ridge constitutes the hanging-wall of a major thrust fault affecting the substratum and separates the south-western and south-eastern branches of the three main NNW-SSE Umbrian basins. The SW branch is bounded to the east by the so-called Martana normal fault, which formed due to the extensional reactivation of a frontal ramp of the Martani Mts. thrusts, during the Lower Pleistocene. The Authors relate the development of the whole Tiber basin to a Lower Pliocene shortening phase, produced by the activity of the thrusts bounding the basin, followed by a new compressive phase, which occurred between Lower and Middle Pleistocene.
In general, they point out that roughly NW-SE normal faults obliquely overprint the NNW trend of the three main branches. For this reason, they relate these normal faults to a younger phase that affected the basin, developing the Anghiari-Sansepolcro and the Bastardo basins, filled by Lower-Middle Pleistocene deposits.
Barchi et al. (1999)
This work focuses on the results of the analysis of the deep reflection seismic profile CROP 03 and of other commercial seismic lines, both orthogonal and parallel to the upper Tiber valley and to the adjacent Umbrian pre-Apennines. The subsurface geometry of the Altotiberina fault is presented in a geological section showing WSW-dipping antithetic faults, the most important of which affects the carbonatic anticlines of Gubbio and Assisi. An isobaths map of the Altotiberina fault was reconstruct and shows a steep shallow trajectory up to 4 km and a flat section between 4 and 6 km. The different dip angle of the fault is related to the different rheology of the involved fault surface formations. Between Umbertide and Perugia the Altotiberina fault seems to deepen and shift westward due to the action of a N-S trending structure, as suggested by the isochronous map. Near Umbertide the thickness of continental sedimentary sequence reaches 1400 m. A regional meaning of the Altotiberina fault, 80 km long and 5 km of maximum offset, is confirmed. The Authors highlight the clear structural continuity between the Altotiberina basin and the Umbria Valley and evidence the analogy of geophysical and geological characters of Massici Perugini and M. Martani, suggesting the existence of such structure along the whole Umbria Valley.
Calamita et al. (1999)
On the basis of structural and geomorphological studies, the Authors pointed out the major steps of Plio-Quaternary tectonic and landscape evolution between the Tiber Valley and the Adriatic coast. The Altotiberina fault is interpreted as related to the instability of the orogenic wedge and is considered to be re-activated from Middle Pliocene. Its activity led to the development of the Tiber basin producing local extensional and compressional structures according to its staircase geometry. NE and SW-dipping normal faults affect the Umbria Valley and are antithetic to the Altotiberina fault. The Authors suggest that such faults present an higher activity, compared with the Altotiberina fault, since 0.7 Ma driven by a N10Â°-20Â° extension coupled with the uplift related to the gravitational collapse of the orogenic wedge.
Boncio et al. (2000a)
This work presents a seismotectonic model in the Umbria-Marche Apennines by integrated analysis of geological, geophysical and seismological data. The recent Norcia, Gubbio and Colfiorito earthquakes as well as a major group of microearthquakes are seen to be compatible with a tensional state of stress, characterised by a NE-trending sub-horizontal sigma 3-axis. This stress tensor, which is parallel to the Plio-Quaternary stress field deduced from fault kinematics, may be considered representative of the mean regional present-day state of stress. The nucleation of most damaging earthquakes is assumed to have occurred at the base of the aftershocks volume, close to the intersection between the SW-dipping antithetic normal faults and the main E-dipping Altotiberina fault. The progressive deepening of the seismicity from the westernmost sectors (Gubbio) to the easternmost ones (Norcia) appears to be well related to the Altotiberina fault basal detachment, as imaged by seismic profiles. An almost continuous microseismic activity (M<3) is spread within the hanging wall volume of the Altotiberina fault. The seismic potential of the active faults is expected to be higher in the easternmost seismic zone, where the detachment is deeper.
Boncio et al. (2000b)
One of the aims of this work is to estimate the seismogenic behaviour of the Altotiberina fault, which activity is still debated. The Authors pointed out the lack of data to state a direct seismogenic role of the Altotiberina fault and to understand if it is mainly creeping, possibly coupled with seismic slip along minor structures, or if it is also able to produce moderate-magnitude or even large earthquakes. In their opinion they cannot exclude that such low-angle fault might be seismogenic along discrete and relatively steep segments, also on its shallowest part. The Altotiberina fault belongs to a regional NE dipping low-angle normal fault system (Etrurian Fault System), which extends for about 350 km from north-western Tuscany to southern Umbria.
Preliminary considerations suggest that the Etrurian Fault System may play an important role in controlling active extension and related seismicity in entire north-central Italy.
Lavecchia et al. (2000)
This work provides a map of the most relevant seismogenic faults of the Umbria-Marche-Abruzzo Apennine coupled with their parameters. An internal alignment of W and SW-dipping, normal faults is evidenced, bounding the eastern side of the Umbria basin, from Mt. Subasio to Spoleto town.
Its continuity, maximum stress orientation, deep geometry and Upper Quaternary activity are considered questionable. Some parameters are suggested to simplify the faults alignment in order to present a tentative seismotectonic zonation: N145Â°-N180Â° strike, SW-W dip, 52 km length, 4 km depth of the seismogenic layer, dip-slip and dip-slip with left component kinematics. The Umbria basin is comprised in a crustal sector, with an ongoing SW-NE maximum extension, in the hanging-wall of the Etrurian Fault System, characterised by widespread micro-seismicity and local moderate earthquake, not larger than magnitude 5.5.
